regions.labelEs: MIS ESTUDIANTES ME HAN METIDO EN OTRA DISCUSIÓN POLÍTICA.

applications.explanationEn: Han changes for the plural students, while metido is the completed-action form of meter.
Me identifies the person drawn in, metido supplies meter in the completed-action form, and en introduces the situation.
A veces marks the event as something that happens on some occasions.

regions.labelEs: ÚLTIMAMENTE ME MOLESTAN LOS DEBATES POLÍTICOS. SÓLO MUESTRAN LO BUENA QUE ES LA GENTE LISTA RACIONALIZANDO.

applications.explanationEn: Lo marks degree, buena gives the feminine description of gente, and que es introduces who has that quality.
The three-word sign names the room reserved for a school's teachers.

regions.labelEs: EL MUNDO ES TAN COMPLICADO QUE CUANTO MÁS APRENDO, MENOS CLARO LO TENGO TODO. HAY DEMASIADAS IDEAS Y ARGUMENTOS DONDE ESCOGER. ¿CÓMO PUEDO CONFIAR EN SABER LA VERDAD SOBRE ALGUNA COSA?

applications.explanationEn: Tan gives the degree of complicado, and que introduces what follows from that degree.
Cuanto más introduces the increasing learning, while menos introduces the decreasing clarity.
Claro is placed first for emphasis, while lo and todo identify what the speaker does not have clearly understood.
Cómo carries an accent because it directly asks how.
Confiar requires en before the trusted action, and saber remains in its unchanged dictionary form.

regions.labelEs: Y SI TODO LO QUE SÉ ES TAN ENDEBLE, ¿QUÉ DEMONIOS HAGO ENSEÑANDO?

applications.explanationEn: Lo que refers neutrally to the whole body of knowledge rather than to a named masculine or feminine noun.
Qué carries an accent because it directly asks what.
Demonios adds exasperated emphasis to the question word qué rather than referring literally to demons.
Enseñando is the -ando form that names the teaching activity occurring while the speaker questions his role.

regions.labelEs: SUPONGO QUE TAN SOLO LO HACES LO MEJOR QUE PUEDES. NADIE PUEDE IMPARTIR VERDADES UNIVERSALES PERFECTAS A SUS ALUMNOS.

applications.explanationEn: Tan solo functions together as the fixed expression “only” here.
Lo mejor que stays fixed, and puedes is the form of poder that matches the person being addressed.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone gets or draws another person into a situation?
cards.answerEn: Use meter a alguien en algo, changing meter for the person and time.
cards.noteEn: Meter literally means “to put.” A introduces the person affected, and en introduces the situation. With a problem, conflict, or activity, the whole pattern can mean to get or drag someone into it.

example.es: No metas a Leo en el problema.
example.en: Don't drag Leo into the problem.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

example.en: I have finished.

cards.noteEn: Metido is the completed-action form of meter. With a person and a situation introduced by en, it can describe getting or drawing that person into the situation.

example.es: Han metido a Leo en un problema.
example.en: They have gotten Leo into a problem.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a veces, “sometimes”

cards.questionEn: How do you say “sometimes” in Spanish?
cards.noteEn: This common time expression describes something that happens on some occasions but not always. It normally sits before or after the verb without changing form.

example.en: Sometimes I cook at home.

cards.noteEn: In frequency expressions such as a veces and algunas veces, English commonly translates the whole expression as “sometimes.”

example.en: I tried it three times.

cards.noteEn: The comic uses the formerly common accent in sólo. Current standard spelling normally writes solo without an accent when it means “only,” unless an accent is exceptionally needed to prevent genuine ambiguity.

example.en: I only need a minute.

cards.answerEn: how; marks the degree of a description in lo ... que

cards.questionEn: How do you express how strikingly good, difficult, large, or similar something is?
cards.answerEn: Use lo, then the describing word, then que and a verb.
cards.noteEn: Each plus sign means “followed by.” Lo stays unchanged, while the adjective—the word that describes a person or thing—matches what it describes: lo bueno for masculine and lo buena for feminine. Que introduces the clause that identifies the person or thing.

example.es: No imaginas lo difícil que es.
example.en: You can't imagine how difficult it is.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes the lo ... que degree pattern

cards.noteEn: Lista can mean “ready” in other contexts. When it describes a person as an ability, it means “smart” or “clever.”

example.en: Marta is very smart.

cards.answerEn: rationalizing; finding plausible reasons after the fact
cards.noteEn: Racionalizando is the -ando form of racionalizar. Here it names the activity at which the people are described as skilled.

example.en: He keeps rationalizing his decision.

cards.questionEn: What does sala de profesores refer to at a school?
cards.answerEn: It is the teachers' lounge or staff room.
cards.noteEn: Sala names a room, de links it to its users, and profesores means teachers here. English naming varies by region between “teachers' lounge” and “staff room.”

example.es: Nos reunimos en la sala de profesores.
example.en: We meet in the staff room.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is so strongly one way that a result follows?
cards.answerEn: Use tan before the describing word, then que before the result.
cards.noteEn: Each plus sign means “followed by.” Tan gives the degree, the adjective describes the person or thing, and que introduces what follows because of that degree.

example.es: La caja es tan pesada que no puedo moverla.
example.en: The box is so heavy that I can't move it.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: the (as part of cuanto más, “the more”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that the more one thing happens, the less another thing happens?
cards.answerEn: Start the first part with cuanto más and the second part with menos.
cards.noteEn: Cuanto has no accent in this comparison because it is not asking “how much.” The verbs and descriptions after más and menos change normally for the people, things, and times involved.

example.es: Cuanto más duermo, menos cansado estoy.
example.en: The more I sleep, the less tired I am.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that you clearly understand or feel sure about something?
cards.noteEn: Tener literally means “to have,” but this pattern says that an idea is clear in someone's mind. Claro can match a named feminine or plural thing: tengo clara la fecha and tengo claras las reglas.

example.es: Tengo clara la fecha de la reunión.
example.en: I'm clear about the meeting date.

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.noteEn: Donde has no written accent here because it links back to the available ideas and arguments rather than asking a direct or indirect question.

example.en: There are several options to choose from.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

example.en: What is your name?

cards.questionEn: What word follows confiar before the person, thing, or action that is trusted?
cards.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” En can introduce a person or thing, or an action verb in its unchanged dictionary form. That unchanged form is called the infinitive and ends in -ar, -er, or -ir.

example.en: I trust that I can finish today.

cards.answerEn: in; required after confiar before what is trusted
what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Lo combines with que to refer to an idea, action, or whole situation rather than a masculine noun. Together, lo que means “what” or “the thing that.”

example.en: I understand what you’re saying.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “what” or “the thing that” without naming a specific object?
cards.answerEn: Use lo que to refer to an idea, action, situation, or unnamed thing.
cards.noteEn: Here lo is neutral: it does not stand for a masculine noun. Que introduces the information that identifies the idea or thing. Together they work as one unit.

example.en: I don't understand what you're saying.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Here que completes lo que, a neutral expression meaning “what” or “the thing that.” It does not refer to a particular masculine or feminine noun.

example.en: I understand what you’re saying.

cards.questionEn: How can you add exasperation or disbelief to a question?
cards.answerEn: Put demonios after qué, dónde, cómo, or another question word.
cards.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” Demonios is not literal here; it adds an informal force similar to “on earth” or, more strongly, “the hell.”

example.en: Where on earth are my keys?

cards.answerEn: on earth; the hell (informal question emphasis)

cards.promptEs: -ando / -iendo para una acción simultánea o un medio
cards.questionEn: How can you add an action that happens at the same time or explains how something is done?
cards.answerEn: Use the action form ending in -ando or -iendo, such as hablando or corriendo.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls this form the gerund. It does not change for the person. Used on its own, it can describe a simultaneous action or the means used: Entró corriendo means the person entered by running. This differs from estar plus the same form, which focuses on an action in progress.

example.en: She came in running.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; adds emphasis in tan solo (“only; just”)

cards.questionEn: How can you say “only” or “just” with a little extra emphasis?
cards.noteEn: Tan solo works as one fixed expression here. Tan does not keep its usual separate meaning “so”; the pair is similar to solamente or solo.

example.en: I have only five minutes.

cards.answerEn: the (neutral article before an adjective, as in lo mejor)
cards.noteEn: Neutral lo turns an adjective into an abstract idea: lo importante means “the important thing,” not a masculine noun.

example.en: The important thing is to begin.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone does something as well as they can?
cards.answerEn: Use lo mejor que followed by a form of poder that matches the person and time.
cards.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” Lo and mejor stay fixed. Poder changes: puedo for “I can,” puedes for “you can,” and podemos for “we can.”

example.en: We cook as well as we can.

cards.noteEn: With el, la, lo, los, or las, mejor usually means “best.” Without one of those words, it often means “better.”

example.en: This is the best option.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: you can; you are able to

cards.noteEn: After a negative verb, nadie is commonly translated as “anyone.” Spanish uses negative concord, so no and nadie can appear together.

example.en: I don’t know anyone.

cards.noteEn: Ejem represents the sound of clearing one's throat, often to attract attention or pointedly interrupt.

example.en: Ahem, I'm still here.
